Compared by eye on the image of PDF page 38 (printed page 31): number 5, the first under the third cluster heading of the fractions domain. The only difference from the record is form: the PDF prints a raised footnote digit (4) after the first sentence, inside the statement, and the record has none; every word, number and sign is equal, the example included, and the statement begins and ends where the record does. The script cannot align the record for that reason, so the offset is left out. The record carries two footnotes and Limits reports both rightly. Its own (mark 4, on this standard): Limits says that children who can make equivalent fractions can work out ways of adding fractions whose denominators differ, and that adding and subtracting such fractions in general is not required in grade 4; that is what the footnote says. The domain's (mark 3, on the domain's name in the heading bar, printed first at the foot of the same page): the new last sentence of Limits names every denominator on the footnote's list, each once and in rising order, nine in all, with none missing and none added; it says that this is another footnote than the first, that it stands on the whole domain and so covers this statement; it adds no other limit and is the pack's own words (the overlap check passes; no run of eight shared words). Remark, not counted a fault: the footnote bounds what is expected in this domain, and the sentence speaks of 'a grade 4 fraction' and gives the domain only as the place where the footnote stands. For this statement the limit is the same; read by itself, the first half of the sentence is wider than the footnote (another domain of the grade has a fraction with a denominator that is not on the list). Read whole: Summary faithful (tenths rewritten as hundredths, and that step used to add one fraction in tenths to one in hundredths; the example kept as an example) and not a near copy. The statement's own two denominators are both on the footnote's list. The cluster heading is given rightly. Worked example right (three tenths are thirty hundredths; with four more, thirty-four).
